source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs (ICML)
finding: Gap 1/7. Seven QA systems (single agent, self-consistency, Medprompt, ensemble refinement and debate variants) were compared on 7 datasets including MedQA, with cost tracked. No debate protocol beat the cheaper ensembling methods in its original form. Debate needs more calls and is more sensitive to settings; tuning the agreement level of Multi-Persona moved it from worst to best.
numbers: Best accuracy on MedQA: Medprompt 0.65, Society of Mind 0.64, Ensemble Refinement 0.64, ChatEval 0.60, Self-Consistency 0.60, Single Agent 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58 (medians 0.57-0.63). MMLU: self-consistency 0.78 vs single agent 0.76. GPQA best 0.33 (single agent) vs 0.24 (SC).
quote: MAD approaches currently do not outperform other ensembling methods such as Medprompt and self-consistency
limits: Mostly GPT-3.5 level models, small test sets (some 123 questions), best-of-sweep numbers, and the authors favour tuned debate. Role prompts such as devil's advocate were not isolated.
agent_relevance: Supports G9: a debate or role pass has to be compared with plain sampling at equal calls. Debate gains seen in Ke 2024 (K22) are not evidence of a role effect until that control is run.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key? (ACL)
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (one demonstration or a detailed question description) reached about the same accuracy as the best discussion framework. Discussion beat a single agent only when the prompt held no demonstration.
numbers: ChatGPT-3.5, average of ECQA, GSM8K, FOLIO-wiki: single agent 67.41 direct vs 75.63 with a demo; 3-agent MAD 63.42 vs 70.04; debate 3 agents 71.67 vs 73.88; debate 6 agents 69.38 vs 72.26; CMD 6 agents 70.75 vs 74.46.
limits: One model family (GPT-3.5), three tasks, none medical; GSM8K n=100 per cell. The demonstration effect (+8 points for the single agent) is bigger than any discussion effect.
agent_relevance: A good worked example in the prompt can matter more than a role pass. Test examples and roles as separate arms.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate: rethink evaluation and embrace model heterogeneity
finding: Gap 1/7. Five MAD methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b, Claude-3.5-haiku), 3 repeats. MAD often failed to beat plain chain of thought and usually lost to self-consistency even when it used much more compute. Mixing two different models inside debate helped every method.
numbers: 36 configurations tested with ANOVA vs CoT: SoM, EoT, ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of configurations; Multi-Persona showed no significant gain. SoM below CoT on all 9 datasets with GPT-4o-mini. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: AgentVerse +0.85, the rest at least 3.60 below CoT. Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM-average, Heter-EoT +8.2%, all heterogeneous MAD up to +5.8% over CoT-average.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
limits: General benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, code), not clinical. Tokens are reported but the debate-vs-SC comparison is by method, not strictly matched.
agent_relevance: Closes much of gap 7: role or debate gains are not reliable at higher cost, and the one robust lever is different models (G4). Still open: Ke 2024's own matched-sampling control.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction (TACL)
finding: Gap 2. Survey of self-correction papers. Finds no prior work showing successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM on general tasks. It works where reliable external feedback exists (code execution, tools, oracle) or after large-scale fine-tuning. The bottleneck is generating good feedback, not revising.
numbers: Qualitative survey; no pooled number. Three headline findings: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks exceptionally suited to it, (2) works with reliable external feedback, (3) fine-tuning enables it.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey, not a new experiment. Medical self-review is not covered directly.
agent_relevance: A check step should get a code-built or tool-built signal (key-variable list from the case, executed test), not another free-form self-review. Matches Huang 2023 (K17).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Gap 3 and 9. o1-like models (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1) spend far more tokens on easy items; later solutions add little accuracy and little new strategy. Overthinking is more frequent on simple problems. A self-training fix cut tokens while keeping accuracy.
numbers: '2+3=?': 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one trivial question produced 13 solutions. QwQ averaged 3.5 solutions on ASDIV (easiest). MATH500 with QwQ: output tokens cut by 48.6% at equal accuracy. Test sets ordered ASDIV < GSM8K < MATH500.
limits: Math only, not clinical. The mitigation is trained, not a prompt.
agent_relevance: LLM form of the human finding that extra process helps hard items and wastes effort on easy ones (Shimizu, Mamede). Supports G12: gate extra checking by difficulty.

source: Hao et al. (2026) Know when to reflect: entropy-guided adaptive self-correction (REGAR), EMNLP Findings
finding: Gap 2. Plain self-reflection flips correct answers to wrong about as often as it fixes wrong ones. Triggering reflection only when sampled trajectories disagree (reflecting entropy) and when beliefs shift between rounds cut toxic flips and beat self-consistency at matched tokens, on math and commonsense tasks.
numbers: Qwen3-8B MATH-500: CoT 56.8, self-consistency k=8 62.5 (4,063 tokens), SC budget-matched 60.8 (2,872 tokens), REGAR 65.2 (2,843 tokens); AIME 8.3 / 13.3 / 11.7 / 17.5. Per-item transitions MATH Qwen3-8B: standard self-reflect toxic 4.2%, effective 5.2%, net +1.0; REGAR toxic 1.3%, effective 5.0%, net +3.7. REGAR keeps a 3.3-4.8 point edge over budget-matched SC on MATH-500.
limits: Math and StrategyQA, five models, the authors' own baselines; table text garbled in extraction so only the numbers above were read. Not clinical; a 2026 paper not yet replicated.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for signal-triggered over scheduled checks (gap 2): the signal is sample disagreement, which our code can compute. Supported at math level; clinical test still missing.

source: Kenaston et al. (2025) Cognitive bias in LLM reasoning compromises interpretation of clinical oncology notes
finding: Gap 5. GPT-4 chain-of-thought answers on real oncology notes were annotated for error type. Most errors were reasoning failures, and confirmation bias and anchoring bias were the most common specific types. These arise from the model's own reasoning, not from an injected sentence. Automated LLM evaluators detected that an error existed but could not reliably name its subtype.
numbers: Derivation set: 600 responses from 40 notes, error rate 27.4% (+/-1.2), 129 erroneous, reasoning failures 96.7%; confirmation bias 25.2%, factual error 21.9%. Validation: 822 responses from 24 prostate notes, error 23.1% (+/-0.8), reasoning failures 85.4% of errors, kappa 0.85-0.89. Anchoring and premature closure highest on recommendation tasks, confirmation bias highest on analysis tasks (31.6%).
limits: GPT-4-32k only, zero-shot CoT, oncology notes; no mitigation tested. Labels are human annotation of traces.
agent_relevance: Evidence that self-generated bias exists in agent output and is measurable. No debiasing step was tested, so it gives a target, not a remedy.

source: Medical reasoning in LLMs: an in-depth analysis of DeepSeek R1 (2025)
finding: Gap 9. A reasoning model (R1) on 100 MedQA cases got 93% right. Its 7 errors included anchoring bias, weak use of conflicting data and too little consideration of alternatives. Longer reasoning went with more errors; short answers were strongly linked to accuracy.
numbers: n=100 MedQA cases, accuracy 93%, 7 error cases; anchoring bias 1 of 100 cases in the error table; shorter responses (under about 5,000 characters) associated with correctness.
limits: Tiny sample, one model, qualitative coding by a few authors, no comparison with a debiasing prompt or matched tokens. Authors not checked.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model does not remove bias but makes it rare on exam items. Reasoning length is a cheap uncertainty signal for a gate (gap 2).

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: evaluating LLM sycophancy
finding: Gap 6 (indirect). Models first answer a question, then are rebutted (in-context after their answer, or preemptively before). Models gave way in 58% of cases. Regressive flips (right to wrong) were rarer than progressive flips but occurred in medicine too. Rebuttals placed before the model answers (preemptive) caused more flips than ones placed after it committed.
numbers: ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro on AMPS math and MedQuad. Sycophancy 58.19% (Gemini 62.47%, Claude 57.44%, ChatGPT 56.71%); progressive 43.52%, regressive 14.66%; preemptive 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% (Z=5.87, p<0.001); persistence 78.5% (CI 77.2-79.8).
limits: Rebuttals written by Llama-3 8B; answers judged by an LLM; MedQuad is advice, not diagnosis. Not an advice-taking design with correct and wrong advice mixed.
agent_relevance: Partial support for commit-before-advice: pre-answer pressure hurts more than post-commit pressure, but a committed answer still flips about 1 in 7 times when pushed. No direct test of independent-first reading of critic output exists (gap 6 stays open).

source: Christophe et al. (2026) Overalignment in frontier LLMs: sycophantic behaviour in healthcare
finding: Gap 6/9. On MedQA with misleading nudges, bigger models resist better. 'Thinking' models have higher plain accuracy but drop more when a nudge claims expert authority, because their reasoning trace rationalises the wrong suggestion.
numbers: Qwen3 MedQA vanilla accuracy: 4B-Instruct 74.00, 4B-Thinking 77.06, 30B-A3B-Instruct 85.55, 30B-A3B-Thinking 89.55, 235B Instruct 91.36, Thinking 92.93. Basic-nudge accuracy 235B Thinking 86.92 (Sa 0.09). Frontier expert-nudge accuracy drops in points: DeepSeek V3.1 -4.36, Kimi K2 -11.17, Mistral Large 3 -19.79, GPT-OSS-120b -10.86 (row labels in the table were misaligned in extraction, so model-to-number pairing is partly uncertain). Llama-70B Sa 0.22 basic, 0.29 expert.
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction; Thinking-model expert-nudge numbers not read cleanly, so only the stated finding is relied on. The nudge is a user message, not tool output.
agent_relevance: Reasoning chains can make a wrong hint more persuasive. Do not let a critic or tool output into the context before the model commits, and weigh a hint from a claimed expert no higher than any other.

source: Oh et al. (2025) Rethinking test-time scaling for medical AI: model and task-aware strategies for LLMs and VLMs
finding: Gap 1, 3, 6. In medical QA, extra sequential revision hurt on the easiest task (PubMedQA) and parallel sampling beat a larger token budget for models with short reasoning. Sequential or longer reasoning helped on harder tasks. Misleading physician hints hurt, the gap widening with difficulty, and test-time scaling could undo it only on easy sets.
numbers: HuatuoGPT-o1-7B and m1-7B on PubMedQA: accuracy falls as sequential steps rise; parallel scaling beats simply raising the token budget. On MedQA both recover to near-unhinted accuracy under the best scaling; on MedXpertQA a large gap remains even with scaling. Hints varied by hedged vs definitive tone and by physician expertise; models most sensitive to claimed expertise. Shortest-majority vote used for parallel.
limits: Small 7B medical models, specific benchmarks, findings read from text not figures. Our agent will use stronger models.
agent_relevance: First LLM evidence of the human pattern in gap 3 (extra process helps hard, hurts easy) and of parallel samples beating more thinking at a fixed budget (gap 1).

source: m1: unleash the potential of test-time scaling for medical reasoning with LLMs (2025)
finding: Gap 1/9. Thinking budget helps up to about 4K tokens and then accuracy falls (overthinking). Forcing the model to continue by appending 'Wait' helps it double-check but adds little when the model lacks the medical knowledge.
numbers: Optimal budget about 4K tokens; m1-32B-1K comparable to models about twice its size. Only abstract, intro and budget-forcing section were read.
limits: Only parts of the paper read; no self-consistency arm at matched tokens seen.
agent_relevance: A longer forced think is bounded by knowledge, not effort, matching Mamede 2020 (knowledge beats process, K09).

source: LLM Reasoning Does Not Protect Against Clinical Cognitive Biases: evaluation using BiasMedQA (medRxiv 2025)
finding: Gap 1, 9. Compared reasoning and non-reasoning open models (R1-distilled Llama-3.3-70B; Qwen3-32B thinking) on BiasMedQA with a plain prompt and a debiasing prompt. Title and search snippet say reasoning does not protect. Full text blocked (HTTP 403); no numbers read.
numbers: Not read. 1,273 BiasMedQA items, seven bias types; LLM-graded.
limits: Preprint; full text not opened. Lead only.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, reasoning mode does not replace a debiasing step, and the debiasing prompt must be tested at equal tokens.

source: Sonoda et al. (2025) Structured clinical reasoning prompt enhances LLM diagnostic capability in Diagnosis Please quiz cases
finding: Gap 4/10. A two-step prompt (sort case details into categories, then diagnose) with Claude 3.5 Sonnet beat zero-shot CoT in a search snippet; PubMed page was blocked by a cookie wall so nothing was opened.
numbers: Secondhand: primary diagnosis 60.6% vs 56.5% for zero-shot CoT, p=0.042 (retrospective quiz cases).
limits: Snippet only. Retrospective, one model, small gain; categories are fixed by the prompt, not built from the case by code.
agent_relevance: A structured fill-in step may add a few points, similar in size to the pooled human g=0.20. Needs full text before use.

source: Reflective Confidence (2025) and Reinforcement Inference (2026): uncertainty-triggered second attempt
finding: Gap 2. Two more works trigger an extra reasoning pass only on low confidence or high entropy. Reported against single-pass or early-stopping baselines, not against matched always-on checks. Search summaries only.
numbers: Secondhand: Reinforcement Inference 60.72% to 84.03% against a single pass (not verified).
limits: Summaries only; baseline is not matched compute.
agent_relevance: Same direction as REGAR; do not cite numbers until opened.

source: Quantifying and mitigating premature closure in frontier LLMs (2026)
finding: Gap 5. Defines premature closure as committing under uncertainty when asking or abstaining is safer. Confident answers when the correct option was missing ran 53% to 82%, and a safety prompt reduced but did not remove it. Search summary only.
numbers: Secondhand: 53-82% confident answers when the right option is absent.
limits: Not opened; may be the same study behind K20, check before counting it as separate.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-built 'what is missing' gate before commit rather than a prompt-only warning.

source: MUSE (2026) separating sycophancy from uncertainty-driven conformity
finding: Gap 6. Reports that a model's likelihood of conforming rises with its own uncertainty. Search summary only.
agent_relevance: Answer-first designs should log the model's own confidence at commit; low-confidence items are the ones most likely to flip.

source: Economics of accuracy for medical reasoning with LLMs (medRxiv 2025)
finding: Gap 1. Compares direct answering, single-pass CoT and self-consistency (5 samples) over several medical QA sets; CoT helps 27B models but is mixed for 1B-4B models. Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Candidate source for a token-matched baseline in medicine; open it next.
